patterns.text: Pattern TP1-01463 (single place). Place: the U.S. state of California (NCA5 region: Southwest). Quantity: fire-weather danger (how hot, dry and windy conditions favour fire). Season: summer. Horizon: by mid-century, compared with the modeled historical baseline. Scenario: under a high-emissions future. Statistic: change of the mean (future minus modeled historical baseline). Direction: increase. Value: +2.2. Mean: 31.4 in the modeled historical baseline, 33.6 at mid-century. Robustness: 2723 of 2831 grid cells change in the same direction as the mean (majority_same_direction). Comparison with other U.S. states: a larger change than in most states (by signed value, among 49 U.S. states for this quantity, season, horizon, scenario and statistic; a relative descriptor among states, not an absolute threshold).

groups.label: strong winds are a primary driver of fire danger and spread

members.statement: Santa Ana wind speed is a primary driver of fire danger, but wind alone cannot produce fire without human ignitions.
members.passage: This study shows that (i) SAW wind speed plays a key role in area burned, (ii) variation in SAW windspeed outweighs fuel characteristics in explaining area burned, (iii) winds alone are insufficient to explain burning without consideration of human ignitions, (iv) ignition sources have changed markedly in recent decades, and (v) autumn and winter temperature and precipitation are less critical tha

members.statement: Higher temperature and stronger wind speed increase wildfire risk on power transmission lines.
members.passage: It is seen that higher temperature and stronger wind speed increase the wildfire risks by the factors of 1.94 (i.e., exp(β 2 )) and 2.43 (i.e., exp(β 3 )). Such findings can be well justified as follows: (i) a higher temperature makes the ignition of the underlying fuels more easily (e.g. grasses, shrubs, dead leaves, etc.), (ii) with an increased wind speed, the electrical conductors and surround

members.statement: Strong winds are identified as a key determinant of large human‑caused wildfires.
members.passage: Common to both events was the occurrence of strong winds that have been shown to be a key determinant in large human-caused wildfires [56].

members.statement: Strong Santa Ana winds, a seasonal weather phenomenon that typically occurs from September to April, are frequently associated with the largest and longest‑duration wildfires in southern California.
members.passage: It has been shown that the largest and longest duration wildfires in southern California are often accompanied by Santa Ana winds [2], a seasonal weather phenomenon affecting southern California from Los Angeles to San Diego that typically occurs from September to April [3,4].

members.statement: Fire spread and the resulting area burnt are driven by wind speed, fire duration, and the amount, moisture content, and characteristics of the fuel, beyond just fire danger.
members.passage: Whereas fire numbers are determined by the presence of fuel, lightning frequency, population density and surface fire intensity, fire spread (and hence area burnt) is driven by wind speed, fire duration and the amount, moisture content and characteristics of the fuel.

groups.label: strong winds and low humidity raise fire danger and fire size

members.statement: Higher maximum wind speeds within a Santa Ana wind event are associated with greater fire danger, leading to larger fires in the 1,000–5,000 ha size class.
members.passage: maximum wind speed was tied to greater area burned by fires in the 1000 to 5000 ha class (Fig. 3B).

members.statement: Meteorology is the dominant control of Santa Ana fires, with fire spread strongly correlated with low relative humidity and strong winds modulated by terrain.
members.passage: Meteorology was clearly the dominant factor controlling SA fires; the spatial and temporal variability of SA FS was well correlated with meteorological drivers, including RH and wind as modulated by terrain (see also figure S3).

members.statement: Low relative humidity and strong wind promote ignition and increase the rate of fire spread within dry fuels, especially for Santa Ana fires.
members.passage: Low relative humidity and strong wind promote ignition and increase the rate of fire spread within dry fuels, especially for SA fires.

members.statement: Fire danger is greater during periods of high temperature, minimal precipitation, low relative humidity and strong winds.
members.passage: While wildfres cannot strictly be defned as meteorological hazards in the same way as droughts, foods and storms, fre danger is greater during periods of high temperature, minimal precipitation, low relative humidity and strong winds.

members.statement: Downslope winds cause adiabatic compression and mixing that inhibit radiative cooling and prevent nocturnal relative humidity recovery, leading to extreme fire weather.
members.passage: The strong winds and adiabatic compression associated with the downslope flow and mixing inhibited radiative cooling and nocturnal RH recovery.

members.statement: Santa Ana wind events are dry, hot Foehn‑type winds that create elevated fire danger, a pattern also observed in other fire‑prone regions such as Europe and Australia.
members.passage: The SA wind events studied here are examples as dry and hot Foehn winds; these winds occur in the leeside of the mountain ranges and are associated with the elevated fire danger in many other parts of the world, including Europe and Australia (Sharples et al 2010).

groups.label: higher temperatures and aridity dry fuels, creating extreme fire‑weather

members.statement: Increasing temperature and aridity have created more frequent extreme fire‑weather conditions, leading to more very large wildfires and higher‑severity burning.
members.passage: Beginning in the late twentieth century, increasing temperature and aridity [23,[59][60][61] have created more frequent extreme fireweather conditions, leading to more very large wildfires [62,63] and area burned at high severity [38,64], although sufficient fuels are necessary for this pattern to continue.

members.statement: Higher temperatures quickly dry wildland fuels, making them easier to ignite and leading to faster fire spread.
members.passage: An increase in the temperature causes the quick drying of wildland fuel, and the drier fuels are easy to ignite and endure a faster rate of fire spread.

members.statement: High temperatures combined with drought-level precipitation and abundant fire‑susceptible fuels create fire‑weather conditions that promote fast‑moving, high‑intensity wildfires.
members.passage: Drought-level rainfall, fire-susceptible vegetation fuels, high temperatures, and strong Santa Ana winds created an ideal fire weather environment for fast moving, high intensity burns.

members.statement: A delayed autumn precipitation combined with unusually warm temperatures kept dead‑fuel moisture at levels typical of midsummer, creating highly flammable conditions.
members.passage: The delayed arrival of autumn precipitation and continued warm temperatures leading up to the fire events allowed for dead fuel moistures to remain at levels more commonly found in mid-to-late summer.

groups.label: humidity and vapor pressure deficit affect fire risk

members.statement: Higher NDVI and higher specific humidity reduce wildfire risk because they indicate healthier, moister vegetation and fewer ignitable fuels.
members.passage: Both the NDVI and the SPFH have negative impacts on wildfire risks, while SPFH has a relatively weaker effect compared with that of NDVI. Note that, a higher NDVI indicates healthier vegetation with more water conditions and fewer potential fuels that can be ignited. Similarly, a high SPFH attaches potential fuels with more moisture, reducing the wildfire risk.

members.statement: Relative humidity and temperature are the most influential individual climate variables affecting observed burned area.
members.passage: Additionally, among the individual climate variables that comprise the FWI, relative humidity and temperature are the most influential factors that affect the observed BA.

members.statement: Forest burned area anomalies are most sensitive to relative humidity anomalies, while non‑forest burned area anomalies are most sensitive to temperature and relative humidity anomalies across most regions.
members.passage: Globally, in the case of forest BA anomaly, the most highly associated climate variable is found to be relative humidity, while in the case of the non-forest BA anomaly, temperature and relative humidity are found to be most highly associated for most of the regions, without, however, exhibiting any clear spatial or latitudinal pattern.

groups.label: warmer atmosphere increases VPD and lowers fuel moisture

members.statement: A warmer atmosphere causes an increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) because saturation vapor pressure exponentially increases with temperature.
members.passage: A warmer atmosphere causes an increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) because saturation vapor pressure exponentially increases with temperature [10].

members.statement: Increases in VPD cause decreases in fuel moisture content.
members.passage: VPD increases cause decreases in fuel moisture content [14].

groups.label: climate change increases extreme fire‑weather frequency

members.statement: Exceptionally warm and dry atmospheric conditions, including high vapor pressure deficit, have driven the recent intensification of wildfire activity in the Western United States.
members.passage: The 2020 wildfire season across the Western U.S. was undoubtedly one for the record books, largely due to exceptionally warm and dry atmospheric conditions [26] in addition to favorable regional wind patterns [2]. According to [26], 2020 ranked as the season with the second highest burned area and vapor pressure deficit-a measure of aridity-across the West over the last 36 years.

members.statement: Climate change in the western United States has increased the frequency of extreme fire weather events and is projected to increase the area burned by wildfire in the coming decades.
members.passage: Climate change in the western United States has increased the frequency of extreme fire weather events and is projected to increase the area burned by wildfire in the coming decades.

members.statement: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency of extreme fire weather and associated smoke events, potentially tripling wildfire numbers by mid‑century.
members.passage: In fact, a 2013 study reported that, based on an ensemble of global climate models, wildfires may triple in number by 2050 leading to substantially higher organic and black carbon concentrations [63].

groups.label: Low sea‑ice concentrations in the Beaufort/Chukchi Seas favor fire‑weather conditions in the western United States.

members.statement: Low sea‑ice concentrations in the Beaufort/Chukchi Seas favor fire‑weather conditions in the western United States.
members.passage: The difference between these simulations bears a strong resemblance to the correlation patterns exhibited by those based on the reanalysis, suggesting that low sea-ice concentrations in the Beaufort/Chukchi Seas favor fire-weather conditions in western states.

groups.scope_phrase: Research on the United States suggests

groups.label: Higher live‑vegetation or dead‑fuel moisture reduces fire hazard

members.statement: Fire sizes increase exponentially with higher VPD and decrease with higher 1000‑hour dead fuel moisture across all spatial scales, especially in forested areas.
members.passage: We find that fire sizes simulated by our model respond, above a threshold, exponentially to increases in VPD and decreases in FM1000 at all spatial scales, although the response is notably stronger in Forests.

groups.scope_phrase: Research on the United States suggests

groups.label: fire weather indices (FWI and components) predict burned area

members.statement: The Fosberg Fire Weather Index (FFWI) is the most important predictor of burned area for Santa Ana fires, explaining the largest share of variance among the variables tested.
members.passage: All models for SA fires identified FFWI as the variable that explained the most variance in burned area (i.e., from 28% of the total model predicted variance in MLR model to 40% for RF; Table 3).

members.statement: The United States, New Zealand and other countries have developed fire danger forecast systems based on the ideas of the FWI.
members.passage: The United States, New Zealand and some others have also successfully formed their own fire danger level forecast systems based on the ideas of the FWI.

members.statement: The Fire Weather Index was calibrated for Canadian jack pine forests but has been shown to perform reasonably well in many dissimilar ecosystems.
members.passage: The FWI (developed in Canada) is specifically calibrated to describe the fire behaviour in a jack pine stand (Pinus banksiana) typical of the Canadian forests. However, its simplicity of implementation has made it a popular choice in many countries, and it has been shown to perform reasonably well in ecosystems very dissimilar to the boreal forest (Di Giuseppe et al., 2016a; de Groot et al., 2007)

members.statement: FWI anomalies correlate strongly with burned area anomalies across many global regions.
members.passage: We find strong correlations of BA anomalies with the FWI anomalies, as well as with the underlying deviations from their climatologies for the four climate variables from which FWI is estimated, namely, temperature, relative humidity, precipitation, and wind.

members.statement: Composite fire danger indices such as the FWI and its sub‑indices correlate better with observed burned area than any single climate variable.
members.passage: We find that the FWI or ISI and BUI subindices typically exhibit stronger correlations to BA than individual climate variables ( figure 3). This indicates that more synthetic variables can be better predictors of BA for the majority of regions.

members.statement: High values of the drought code and duff moisture code, components of the FWI, are common factors in recent large fires worldwide.
members.passage: High values of the drought code (DC) and the duff moisture code (DMC), which are components of the FWI, are some of the common factors in the large fires that have recently burned in many regions of the world.

members.statement: Drought‑related fire‑weather variables, especially the Duff Moisture Code (DMC) and the Buildup Index (BUI), are the most important factors for supporting overnight burning events across all biome‑season groups.
members.passage: The results indicated that drought-related variables played a crucial role in supporting OBEs (Fig. 4).Specifically, either DMC or BUI was found to be the most important factor in all groups.

groups.label: fuel moisture is estimated from soil moisture or weather and strongly controls fire emissions

members.statement: Live fuel moisture is estimated from soil moisture, while dead fuel moisture is derived directly from climatic inputs, influencing fire behavior.
members.passage: The moisture content of the live fuel classes is estimated from soil moisture provided by the biogeochemical module. Dead fuel moisture content is estimated directly from climatic inputs (Cohen and Deeming 1985).

members.statement: Dead fine fuel moisture content (DFMC) is mainly governed by weather conditions and therefore changes rapidly on hourly to daily time scales.
members.passage: Contrary to LFMC, the DFMC is mainly governed by weather conditions and for that reason it is changing at a fast pace (hourly and daily fluctuations) during the day, causing significant alterations in the forest fuel's flammability levels [31][32][33].

members.statement: Fuel moisture, as captured by dynamic weather modelling, strongly influences fuel consumption rates and therefore fire emissions.
members.passage: This was largely due to the impact of fuel moisture on consumption rates as captured by the dynamic weather modelling.

groups.label: fire‑danger indices are defined/measured from weather variables and intermediate moisture variables

members.statement: Fire events are triggered in the model when the Build Up Index and the Fine Fuel Moisture Code (BUI and FFMC of the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System) meet set thresholds.
members.passage: Fire events are triggered in the model when the Build Up Index and the Fine Fuel Moisture Code (BUI and FFMC of the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System) meet set thresholds.

members.statement: Local noon station values are used to calculate the current and forecast fire weather indices as described by the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI) System (Van Wagner 1987); station values are then interpolated spatially to produce daily fire weather maps.
members.passage: Local noon station values are used to calculate the current and forecast fire weather indices as described by the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI) System (Van Wagner 1987); station values are then interpolated spatially to produce daily fire weather maps.
members.region: Canada and the continental United States

members.statement: Fire danger indices compute intermediate variables that correspond to measurable quantities such as dead‑fuel moisture, live‑fuel moisture, and slope effect, preserving interpretability.
members.passage: Most of these intermediate variables have concrete meaning and could be measured. For example, 1-hour, 10-hour, 100-hour, and 1000-hour deadfuels moisture (which represent wildland fuels whose moisture contents are controlled entirely by changing weather conditions), live-fuel moisture variables, reaction velocity, slope effect, and many others.

members.statement: The internal variables of fire danger indices, such as equilibrium moisture content and slope effect coefficient, are meaningful and can be measured, unlike hidden layers in typical neural networks.
members.passage: Internally, these fire index models compute intermediate variables which are combined to produce a set of fire danger indices. These internal variables are meaningful in that they correspond to (possibly) measurable quantities; e.g., the equilibrium moisture content, which represents the steady state moisture content of woody material, and the slope effect coefficient, among many others.

members.statement: Fire danger systems are based primarily on empirical models of weather effects on the moisture content and flammability of various organic layers.
members.passage: Much early fire research in North America focused on the development of fire danger rating systems that were designed to capture the cumulative effects of weather in numerical measures of daily fire potential (Taylor and Alexander (2006); Hardy and Hardy (2007)).

members.statement: Expected fire threat level can be parameterized by modeling radiative energy transfer or reaction intensity, or by using composite fire‑danger indices.
members.passage: The expected fire threat level at each household, as well as for each refuge shelter and along evacuation routes, could be parameterized directly by modeling radiative energy transfer based on temperature [63] or reaction intensity [64], or indirectly by using an index that combines multiple energy transfer factors (e.g., [65]).

guardrails: A modeled historical baseline is model output for a past period, not an observation.
A Fire Weather Index is a meteorological fire-danger index; it is never fire occurrence, ignition, burned area or damage.
A high-emissions future is one plausible future, not a forecast and not the only plausible future.
Hazard is not exposure, and exposure is not risk.

members.statement: Fire danger indices compute intermediate variables that correspond to measurable quantities such as dead‑fuel moisture, live‑fuel moisture, and slope effect, preserving interpretability.
members.verbatim_passage: Most of these intermediate variables have concrete meaning and could be measured. For example, 1-hour, 10-hour, 100-hour, and 1000-hour deadfuels moisture (which represent wildland fuels whose moisture contents are controlled entirely by changing weather conditions), live-fuel moisture variables, reaction velocity, slope effect, and many others.

members.statement: The internal variables of fire danger indices, such as equilibrium moisture content and slope effect coefficient, are meaningful and can be measured, unlike hidden layers in typical neural networks.
members.verbatim_passage: Internally, these fire index models compute intermediate variables which are combined to produce a set of fire danger indices. These internal variables are meaningful in that they correspond to (possibly) measurable quantities; e.g., the equilibrium moisture content, which represents the steady state moisture content of woody material, and the slope effect coefficient, among many others.

members.statement: Fire danger systems are based primarily on empirical models of weather effects on the moisture content and flammability of various organic layers.
members.verbatim_passage: Much early fire research in North America focused on the development of fire danger rating systems that were designed to capture the cumulative effects of weather in numerical measures of daily fire potential (Taylor and Alexander (2006); Hardy and Hardy (2007)).

members.statement: Expected fire threat level can be parameterized by modeling radiative energy transfer or reaction intensity, or by using composite fire‑danger indices.
members.verbatim_passage: The expected fire threat level at each household, as well as for each refuge shelter and along evacuation routes, could be parameterized directly by modeling radiative energy transfer based on temperature [63] or reaction intensity [64], or indirectly by using an index that combines multiple energy transfer factors (e.g., [65]).

LG-fire_weather_v1-driver-c1-003: strong winds are a primary driver of fire danger and spread
Santa Ana wind speed is a primary driver of fire danger, but wind alone cannot produce fire without human ignitions.
Higher temperature and stronger wind speed increase wildfire risk on power transmission lines.
Strong winds are identified as a key determinant of large human‑caused wildfires.
Strong Santa Ana winds, a seasonal weather phenomenon that typically occurs from September to April, are frequently associated with the largest and longest‑duration wildfires in southern California.
Fire spread and the resulting area burnt are driven by wind speed, fire duration, and the amount, moisture content, and characteristics of the fuel, beyond just fire danger.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c1-002: strong winds and low humidity raise fire danger and fire size
Higher maximum wind speeds within a Santa Ana wind event are associated with greater fire danger, leading to larger fires in the 1,000–5,000 ha size class.
Meteorology is the dominant control of Santa Ana fires, with fire spread strongly correlated with low relative humidity and strong winds modulated by terrain.
Low relative humidity and strong wind promote ignition and increase the rate of fire spread within dry fuels, especially for Santa Ana fires.
Fire danger is greater during periods of high temperature, minimal precipitation, low relative humidity and strong winds.
Downslope winds cause adiabatic compression and mixing that inhibit radiative cooling and prevent nocturnal relative humidity recovery, leading to extreme fire weather.
Santa Ana wind events are dry, hot Foehn‑type winds that create elevated fire danger, a pattern also observed in other fire‑prone regions such as Europe and Australia.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c1-003: higher temperatures and aridity dry fuels, creating extreme fire‑weather
Increasing temperature and aridity have created more frequent extreme fire‑weather conditions, leading to more very large wildfires and higher‑severity burning.
Higher temperatures quickly dry wildland fuels, making them easier to ignite and leading to faster fire spread.
High temperatures combined with drought-level precipitation and abundant fire‑susceptible fuels create fire‑weather conditions that promote fast‑moving, high‑intensity wildfires.
A delayed autumn precipitation combined with unusually warm temperatures kept dead‑fuel moisture at levels typical of midsummer, creating highly flammable conditions.
LG-fire_weather_v1-driver-c1-002: humidity and vapor pressure deficit affect fire risk
Higher NDVI and higher specific humidity reduce wildfire risk because they indicate healthier, moister vegetation and fewer ignitable fuels.
Relative humidity and temperature are the most influential individual climate variables affecting observed burned area.

Forest burned area anomalies are most sensitive to relative humidity anomalies, while non‑forest burned area anomalies are most sensitive to temperature and relative humidity anomalies across most regions.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c1-001: warmer atmosphere increases VPD and lowers fuel moisture
A warmer atmosphere causes an increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) because saturation vapor pressure exponentially increases with temperature.
Increases in VPD cause decreases in fuel moisture content.
LG-fire_weather_v1-driver-c1-006: climate change increases extreme fire‑weather frequency
Exceptionally warm and dry atmospheric conditions, including high vapor pressure deficit, have driven the recent intensification of wildfire activity in the Western United States.
Climate change in the western United States has increased the frequency of extreme fire weather events and is projected to increase the area burned by wildfire in the coming decades.
Climate change is expected to increase the frequency of extreme fire weather and associated smoke events, potentially tripling wildfire numbers by mid‑century.
LG-fire_weather_v1-driver-c2-021: Low sea‑ice concentrations in the Beaufort/Chukchi Seas favor fire‑weather conditions in the western United States.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c2-004: Higher live‑vegetation or dead‑fuel moisture reduces fire hazard
Fire sizes increase exponentially with higher VPD and decrease with higher 1000‑hour dead fuel moisture across all spatial scales, especially in forested areas.
LG-fire_weather_v1-driver-c1-005: fire weather indices (FWI and components) predict burned area
The Fosberg Fire Weather Index (FFWI) is the most important predictor of burned area for Santa Ana fires, explaining the largest share of variance among the variables tested.
The United States, New Zealand and other countries have developed fire danger forecast systems based on the ideas of the FWI.
The Fire Weather Index was calibrated for Canadian jack pine forests but has been shown to perform reasonably well in many dissimilar ecosystems.
FWI anomalies correlate strongly with burned area anomalies across many global regions.
Composite fire danger indices such as the FWI and its sub‑indices correlate better with observed burned area than any single climate variable.
High values of the drought code and duff moisture code, components of the FWI, are common factors in recent large fires worldwide.

Drought‑related fire‑weather variables, especially the Duff Moisture Code (DMC) and the Buildup Index (BUI), are the most important factors for supporting overnight burning events across all biome‑season groups.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c1-007: fuel moisture is estimated from soil moisture or weather and strongly controls fire emissions
Live fuel moisture is estimated from soil moisture, while dead fuel moisture is derived directly from climatic inputs, influencing fire behavior.
Dead fine fuel moisture content (DFMC) is mainly governed by weather conditions and therefore changes rapidly on hourly to daily time scales.
Fuel moisture, as captured by dynamic weather modelling, strongly influences fuel consumption rates and therefore fire emissions.
LG-fire_weather_v1-mechanism-c1-004: fire‑danger indices are defined/measured from weather variables and intermediate moisture variables
